opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is more subtle than people usually assume. The common story is that large language models are the ultimate vindication of the bitter lesson: you stop hand-engineering, scale up data and compute with a general method, and capability emerges. In one sense that's true. Next-token prediction on internet-scale text with Transformers is about as general and scalable as it gets.

But I think if you read Rich Sutton's essay carefully, the deeper point isn't "make the model bigger." It's that methods which **leverage computation through search and learning from experience** win over methods that bake in human knowledge. And from that angle, language models are a bit of a paradox. The architecture is general, but the data is entirely human knowledge. Language is already a highly compressed, curated product of human thinking. So in some ways, LLMs are the biggest exercise in *distilling human priors* we've ever done. We just moved the human engineering out of the model and into the data.

That has consequences. When you train on text, you're bounded by what humans have written down, and how they chose to describe the world. That's why we're now talking about running out of high-quality data, and why so much effort goes into synthetic data, RLHF, and reasoning traces. Those are all, in a sense, ways of injecting more human guidance back in.

Coming from computer vision, I tend to think the more "bitter-lesson-aligned" path eventually has to involve learning from raw sensory experience: video, interaction, the physical world. That signal is far richer than text, it isn't pre-digested by humans, and it scales in a way language doesn't. The catch is that it's much harder. We don't yet have the equivalent of next-token prediction for vision that works as cleanly. Visual representation learning is still an open problem, and I think that's exactly why it's interesting.

So my view is: LLMs proved the scaling half of the bitter lesson spectacularly. But the other half, learning from experience rather than from our own descriptions of the world, is still largely ahead of us. I don't think language is the end point. It's an extremely powerful shortcut, and shortcuts are exactly what the bitter lesson warns us to be humble about.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs distill human priors and place human knowledge in the training data, which conflicts with the bitter lesson’s emphasis on learning from experience rather than relying on human knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Thanks for having me. I think of the bitter lesson as a statement that's been proven right over and over, but people tend to read it in a shallow way. The headline version is "scale beats human priors," and large language models look like the ultimate confirmation of that: you take a simple objective, next-token prediction, you throw a huge amount of data and compute at it, and suddenly capabilities emerge that decades of hand-designed systems never achieved. On that level, yes, LLMs are the bitter lesson playing out in the most dramatic way we've ever seen.

But I'd push back a little on the triumphalist reading. Rich Sutton's point was never that human knowledge is useless. It was that we should put our effort into methods that improve with compute, rather than baking in what we currently believe about the problem. And if you actually look at how LLMs got built, there was an enormous amount of human judgment involved. The transformer is an architectural decision. The tokenizer is a prior. The choice to train on language at all, the way data is filtered and curated, instruction tuning, RLHF, all of that is people deciding what the system should learn from and how. So the lesson isn't "remove the human." It's "move the human to the right level of abstraction." You stop hand-coding the solution and start designing the conditions under which the solution can be discovered.

Coming from the vision side, this is something I think about a lot. In vision we went through our own version of this. We used to design features, then we learned features but designed architectures, then with ConvNeXt and the transformer work we started realizing that a lot of the architectural differences people argued about mattered much less than the training recipe and the scale. Each time, the thing that felt like our expertise turned out to be a bottleneck. That's the bitter part. It's bitter because it's humbling.

Where I think the story is still open is in what happens when language data runs out, or when you move to domains where the data isn't already a compressed record of human thought. Text is special. Humans spent thousands of years writing down what they know, so an LLM is scaling against a very dense signal. The visual world doesn't come with that annotation. So when people say the bitter lesson implies that vision, robotics, world models will just fall out of scaling the same way, I'm more cautious. Scaling will matter, I'm sure of that, but figuring out what to scale and what signal to learn from is still a research problem, and that part is not something you can brute-force. In a sense the bitter lesson tells you which direction to walk, but it doesn't tell you where the road is.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs are a dramatic confirmation of the bitter lesson, not that they run counter to it.

astra-6.text:
I think large language models are a very compelling example of the bitter lesson. You have a fairly general learning method, and instead of trying to encode everything we know about language into the system, you let it learn from data at scale. As you increase the compute and the data, capabilities emerge that would be very difficult to engineer one by one.

But I don’t interpret the bitter lesson as saying that research or human insight doesn’t matter. The question is where you put that insight. Are you designing a system around your assumptions about how a particular task should be solved, or are you designing a learning process that can discover better solutions as you give it more resources? There’s a lot of ingenuity in making the second approach work.

And it doesn’t mean that the current architecture is the final answer. That would actually be a strange conclusion to draw from the bitter lesson. We should keep looking for methods that learn more effectively and scale better, rather than becoming too attached to the particular recipe that happens to work today.

r001.rationale: The response calls large language models a compelling example of the bitter lesson, rather than asserting that they run counter to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think large language models are a very strong example of the bitter lesson. The idea is that general methods that can take advantage of more computation tend to win over approaches where we try to encode a lot of human knowledge by hand. With language models, you have a fairly general architecture, a simple training objective, and enormous amounts of data and compute—and surprisingly broad capabilities emerge.

But I wouldn’t interpret that as saying research doesn’t matter, or that we should just make everything bigger. The question is: what kinds of research continue to pay off as you scale? Choosing the architecture, the learning objective, and how you use computation still matters enormously. You want your ideas to enable scaling, rather than impose assumptions that eventually become a bottleneck.

And language models don’t establish that the current recipe is the final answer. They demonstrate how powerful scalable learning can be. There’s still room to discover more general, more efficient ways to learn.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly calls large language models a strong example of the bitter lesson, rather than saying they run counter to it.
